qt: to the Commission Daniel Freund (Verts/ALE), Terry Reintke (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In February each year, neo-Nazi marches glorifying National Socialism are held in Budapest on the so-called ‘Day of Honour’. This year once more, thousands of people, many of whom travelled from all over Europe, took part in a Waffen SS memorial march. Swastikas and Nazi symbols can be worn openly, and the march is state-sponsored through Hungarian Government ministries. Weapons, uniforms and Nazi memorabilia are officially provided by the Military History Museum. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these marches and the Hungarian Government’s support for them?
Is the Commission aware that the Hungarian authorities tolerate the use of symbols which are incompatible with the EU's fundamental rights?
What is the Commission doing to ensure respect for the EU’s fundamental rights in Hungary during the so-called 'Day of Honour'?
at: (English version) to the Commission Daniel Freund (Verts/ALE), Terry Reintke (Verts/ALE) (21 March 2024) Subject: Neo-Nazi marches glorifying National Socialism in Budapest on the ‘Day of Honour’ In February each year, neo-Nazi marches glorifying National Socialism are held in Budapest on the so-called ‘Day of Honour’. This year once more, thousands of people, many of whom travelled from all over Europe, took part in a Waffen SS memorial march. Swastikas and Nazi symbols can be worn openly, and the march is state-sponsored through Hungarian Government ministries. Weapons, uniforms and Nazi memorabilia are officially provided by the Military History Museum. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these marches and the Hungarian Government’s support for them?

2. Is the Commission aware that the Hungarian authorities tolerate the use of symbols which are incompatible with the EU's fundamental rights? 3. What is the Commission doing to ensure respect for the EU’s fundamental rights in Hungary during the so-called ‘Day of Honour’? (17 June 2024) The Commission is aware of the ‘Day of Honour’ marches. Member States have the exclusive competence to authorise or prohibit such marches, in accordance with Article 72 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Generally, the Commission finds these events deeply concerning, in particular the use of violent right-wing extremist symbols. The Commission is fully committed to using its competencies to ensure the respect of fundamental rights in all Member States, including Hungary, and safeguarding the values of equality and respect for human dignity, as enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union. As stated in the EU Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (1), Nazi-related symbols, memorabilia and literature may constitute hate speech under national laws implementing the framework Decision when publicly inciting hatred and violence (2). The Commission cooperates with industry and IT companies to prevent the illegal display and sale of such items online. The Commission supports Member States in the fight against violent right-wing extremism using all instruments in place in line with the four strands of work enshrined in the 2019 Council conclusions on right-wing violent extremism and terrorism (3). Among others, the Commission supported the creation of a non-legally binding working definition of violent right-wing extremism (4) and promoted the use of the Radicalisation Awareness Network to boost knowledge sharing in this area (5). The EU Internet Forum (6) assembled a list of violent right-wing extremist groups and symbols banned in EU Member States and shared it with online platform to support their content moderation efforts.
